en: Points of Controversy The Chapter on Refutation The Twentieth Section
The Discussion on Unintentional Action:
Is one subject to an immediate retribution (ānantarika) after depriving one’s mother of life unintentionally? Yes.
"Is one who kills a living being unintentionally still a killer?
"One should not say so...
"...is one who deprives his mother of life unintentionally an immediate offender?"
“Yes,” he said.
“Having intentionally taken what is not given … having spoken falsehood, does one become a liar?”
It should not be said thus … [as before] … Having unintentionally killed a living being, is one not a killer of living beings? Yes.
If one has deprived one's mother of life unintentionally, does it not constitute an immediate offense (*ānantarika*)?
One should not say so …pe… if one has taken what was not given unintentionally …pe…
Is it the case that one who speaks falsely is not a liar? Yes.
Is it the case that one who has intentionally deprived his mother of life does not incur an immediate retribution (*ānantarika*)? No.
It should not be said thus … [as before] … Having intentionally deprived one’s mother of life, does one become an ānantarika (one who commits an immediate offense)? Yes.
“Is there such a sutta as: ‘Having intentionally deprived one’s mother of life, one becomes an immediate offender’?”—
It does not exist.
“Having intentionally deprived one’s mother of life, one becomes an ānantarika”—
is there indeed such a sutta?
Yes, there is.
If it is true that there is indeed a sutta stating, "Having intentionally deprived one's mother of life,
one becomes an immediate offender," then surely, O sir, you ought not say:
"Having unintentionally deprived one's mother of life, one becomes an immediate offender."
Is it not to be said that "a matricide is one who commits an immediate offense"?
Yes, it is.
"Is it not the case that a mother has been deprived of life?
"Yes.
"If indeed a mother has been deprived of life, then, indeed, it must be said—"
“Is it not to be said that ‘one who kills his mother is an immediate offender’? “No;
it is to be said that ‘one who kills his father is an immediate offender.’”
“Yes.
“But has his father not been deprived of life?
“Yes.”
If the father has been deprived of life, then indeed it should be said:
"The patricide is one who commits an immediate offense.
It should not be said [that he is not].
“Is a murderer of an arahant one who commits an immediate offense?”—
“Yes.”—
“But has not an arahant been deprived of life?”
“Yes.
“If an arahant has been deprived of life, then indeed it must be said:
‘The murderer of an arahant is one who commits an immediate offense.’”
Is it not to be said that one who causes the shedding of blood incurs immediate retribution?
Yes, it is.
"But was not the Tathāgata’s blood shed?
"Yes.
"If the Tathāgata’s blood was indeed shed, then, alas, you must surely say this:"
“An offender who causes the shedding of blood is one for whom there is immediate retribution. Is an offender who causes a schism in the Saṅgha one for whom there is immediate retribution?
Yes, he is.
Are all those who cause a schism in the Saṅgha creators of an immediate offense?
One should not say so... [and so on] ...
Are all those who cause a schism in the Saṅgha creators of an immediate offense?
“Yes.
[The opponent asks: “Is one who causes a schism in the Saṅgha while perceiving it as a [legitimate] Dhamma an ānantarika?
“It should not be said so,” and so forth.
"One who causes a schism in the Saṅgha while perceiving [the person] as a Dhamma-possessor is an ānantarika, is he not?
"Yes.
"But was it not said by the Blessed One—"
“Upāli, one who causes a schism in the Saṅgha is destined for the states of deprivation, destined for hell, staying there for an eon, and incurable.
Upāli, one who causes a schism in the Saṅgha is not destined for the states of deprivation, not destined for hell, does not stay there for an eon, and is not incurable.
Is this indeed a sutta?
“Yes, [it is so].
Therefore, it should not be said:
“One who causes a schism in the Saṅgha while perceiving it as the Dhamma incurs an immediate offense.”
Is it not to be said that one who causes a schism in the Saṅgha while perceiving it as the Dhamma incurs an immediate retribution?
Yes, it is.
Has it not been said by the Blessed One:
“One who causes a schism in the Saṅgha is destined for the states of misery, destined for hell, remaining there for an eon”?
Delighting in factions and established in unrighteousness,
one falls away from security from bondage;
having split a harmonious Saṅgha, one...
“He will be cooked in hell for an eon.
Is this indeed a sutta?
Yes, it is.
Therefore, it is said that "one who causes a schism in the Saṅgha is an ānantarika.
The discussion on unintentional action is finished.
